Fermi GBM  ·  ground localization check

Lining up a DoL reproduction with GBM's official positions

Gamma-ray bursts drawn at random from the Fermi GBM catalog, each localized from scratch with the legacy Daughter-of-Locburst grid search and compared against the official GBM HEALPix map. Choosing the source window the way a Burst Advocate does, rather than using the whole T90 interval, cuts the median gap from 4.58° to 2.40° across 22 bursts. Narrowing the energy band, the obvious next lever, does not help at all.

4.58°2.40° median separation, 22 bursts pooled
10.74°3.82° mean separation
14/22 bursts improved by the window change
1.66° best energy band is the standard one

What this tests

The official GBM map and this reproduction run the same algorithm on the same data. Neither uses information from any other observatory: the FITS header of every official map records LOC_SRC = 'Fermi, GBM'. The only cross-mission ingredient anywhere in the chain is the systematic error model, calibrated once, population-wide, against bursts with precise positions from Swift and others — it widens the probability region but never moves the centroid of an individual burst.

So a disagreement cannot come from the official map knowing something this one doesn't. It can only come from the choices a human Burst Advocate normally makes by hand. That makes this a clean experiment: change one choice, and the separation column measures exactly how much it was worth.

What closed the gap

The first pass localized on the catalog's full T90 interval. That is the defensible automatic choice, and it is wrong for the job. T90 is a duration measurement — the span containing the middle 90% of the fluence — not a statement about where the signal is strong. On a burst with a bright spike and a long soft tail, most of T90 contributes background and almost no signal.

The grid search weighs each detector's net counts against its background. Padding the window with near-empty time dilutes the very contrast the fit depends on: the region inflates, and the centroid is free to drift.

The change: instead of the full T90, take the contiguous sub-interval that maximises sum(net) / sqrt(sum(background)) over the summed triggered detectors in the 50–300 keV band. Every contiguous bin range inside the burst is tested; the best-S/N one wins. Background windows are untouched, so the two runs differ in exactly one choice.

Median separation falls from 3.04° to 1.66° and the mean from 4.46° to 2.02°. The worst case drops from 12.89° to 4.15°, which matters more than the median: the long tail of bad localizations is what made the first pass untrustworthy, and it is gone. 6 of 10 bursts improved, 3 regressed slightly.

Does it hold up on bursts it was not tuned on?

The window rule was chosen after looking at the first ten bursts, so measuring it on those same ten proves nothing. A second sample was drawn with a different seed and run untouched.

Sample Bursts Median, T90 window Median, best S/N Improved
A — the one shown below 10 3.04° 1.66° 6/10
B — held out, fresh seed 12 6.53° 3.71° 8/12
Pooled 22 4.58° 2.40° 14/22

The window change reproduces: 8 of 12 held-out bursts improved, and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test over all 22 pairs gives p = 0.017. Because the comparison is paired on identical bursts, it does not care how either sample happened to be composed.

The absolute number is less certain than it looks. Sample A alone gave a median of 3.04° before the change and 1.66° after; sample B, the same method, gave 6.53° and 3.71°. Bootstrapping the pooled results, the median of a random ten-burst draw spans roughly 1.8–3.5°. Sample A was on the fortunate side of that, so the pooled 2.40° is the figure to quote — not the number from any single draw.

Narrowing the energy band does not help

If restricting in time bought that much, restricting in energy is the obvious thing to try next. It does not work, and the failure is informative.

Trigdat carries only eight coarse channels, so the band is not continuously tunable — the standard 50–300 keV lands on channels 3–4, and only a handful of genuinely distinct bands exist. Every narrowing is worse, and the single-channel bands are roughly three times worse: 1.66° becomes 4.45° using 44–95 keV alone, or 3.60° using 95–300 keV alone.

The reason is the opposite of the time case. The grid search infers position from the contrast in counts across the twelve NaI detectors, whose angular responses differ. Trimming in time removed intervals that carried background but no signal. Trimming in energy removes real signal from every detector at once, so the contrast the fit depends on gets noisier while nothing useful is discarded.

Widening to 44–500 keV looked marginally better on sample A (1.60° against 1.66°), so it was checked on the held-out sample: better on only 5 of 12 bursts, with a worse maximum on both samples. That is a coin flip, and the apparent gain came from one burst moving 9.97° to 1.08°. GBM's standard band stands.

Reading the figures

Red is this reproduction. Blue is the official GBM map. Solid contours are 90% confidence, dashed are 50%. The black star is the catalog position.

Each burst shows its lightcurve with both candidate windows marked, then the localization before and after the change, then an all-sky frame for context. The close-ups are where agreement is readable — at all-sky scale a couple of degrees is nearly invisible.

What the numbers mean, and what they don't

This is agreement, not identity

The pooled median of 2.40° sits inside GBM's own systematic error, whose core for this model is a 2.3–4.2° Gaussian depending on where the burst falls in spacecraft azimuth. The reproduction tracks the official pipeline to within its stated uncertainty — it is not, and cannot be made, pixel-identical, because the remaining difference is a human's judgement about where a burst starts and stops.

The window change is not free

7 of 22 bursts regressed. A pure maximum-S/N criterion is a reasonable stand-in for a Burst Advocate, not a replica of one: a real BA also weighs spectral hardness and detector geometry, and knows when a window has become too short to be worth trimming further. The regressions cluster where the rule has least to work with — very short bursts, and very long ones where the selected window is still most of T90 and the change is mostly noise.

My regions are still larger than the official ones

On sample A the median area ratio improved from 1.53x to 1.30x but did not reach parity. Some of this is irreducible without matching the official pipeline's exact interval, and some of it is conservative in the right direction: a region that is too large is honest about uncertainty, where one that is too small is not.

Short bursts do markedly worse

Sample A drew 10 long bursts and no short ones; the held-out sample supplied the first three. They land at a median of 6.36° against 2.15° for the 19 long bursts. Three is far too few to put a number on, but the direction is what you would expect: a short burst gives the fit a fraction of the counts, so the detector-to-detector contrast it works from is correspondingly noisier.

One short burst, bn251220985 (T90 0.38 s), is also the worst regression anywhere in this work — 3.08° to 12.52°. S/N maximisation trimmed its window to 0.2 s, and at that duration there are too few counts left to localize on. The window rule needs a floor for short bursts; it does not have one here.

The systematic model could not be matched per burst

The intent was to pick hitl_model or robo_ba_model per burst from each official map's LMETHOD header, since the two describe differently shaped error distributions. In practice all 2,061 official HEALPix files in the archive carry LMETHOD = 'Interactive' — written unconditionally, recording nothing about whether a human or the robot produced the map. Every burst here therefore uses hitl_model. For any map that was in fact RoboBA output, the other kernel would have been more appropriate and the area comparison would shift.

Centroid is not the same quantity as catalog position

The official map's centroid sits 0.26–1.31° from the position listed in the burst catalog for the same burst. These are genuinely different quantities — the probability-weighted centre of an Earth-occultation-removed map, versus the quoted best-fit position — so the comparison here is centroid against centroid throughout.

Reproducing this

Pipeline and provenance
  • Burst list: HEASARC fermigbrst via TAP, 4,400 GRBs spanning 2008-07-14 to 2026-10-20.
  • Data: glg_trigdat_all_* and glg_healpix_all_* for every catalog burst, 5.2 GB from the HEASARC trigger tree.
  • Eligible pool: 2,061 bursts with both an official HEALPix map and a usable T90. Official maps exist only from roughly 2018 onward; earlier bursts carry a glg_locprob_all_* gnomonic image instead, or no map at all, and cannot be compared this way.
  • Sample: 10 drawn without replacement, seed 20261022. Both runs use the identical sample.
  • Localization: legacy_DoL from astro-gdt-fermi, atmospheric scattering enabled, 50–300 keV, detector mask set internally by the routine (NaI with background above 100 counts/s, both BGOs excluded).

One correction was needed to the reference implementation before it could survive long bursts at all. legacy_DoL expects count rates, not counts — it multiplies the input by the source duration internally. Passing counts is harmless for a 2 s window, where the error is a common factor that cancels in the flux normalisation, and both conventions agree to the digit on bn200826187. Over a 100 s window the same mistake inflates every chi-square past the routine's internal clamp, leaving the grid uniform and the search dead on an empty argmin.

Built 2026-10-22 from locally archived Fermi GBM data. Figures generated with astro-gdt-fermi; probability maps are HEALPix, NSIDE 128, equatorial coordinates.
